title: The empty row at the back

lines.text: The plateau is in its third week of heat and Schuman is the only room on this floor whose air conditioning works, which is most of why nineteen people are in it. Gantt has laid a printed agenda on every chair. Nobody has picked one up.
lines.plain: Luxembourg is in its third week of hot weather. Schuman is the only room on this floor with working air conditioning. That is one reason nineteen people are here. Gantt put a printed agenda on every chair. Nobody has taken one.

lines.text: Ninety minutes. I will chair.
lines.plain: You have ninety minutes. I will lead the meeting.

lines.text: The agenda went out on the third with the Handbook and the Work Plan. Nobody commented. I run it. You do the two minutes at the end that only you can do.
lines.plain: I sent the agenda on 3 July, with the Project Handbook and the Project Work Plan. Nobody sent comments. I will lead the meeting. At the end you speak for two minutes, because only you can say that part.
ref: Project Manager (PM) — Organises the meeting.

lines.text: Which two minutes?
lines.plain: Which two minutes do you mean?

lines.text: The ones where the Project Owner says out loud, to forty people, that the fifteenth of May 2028 is not a target.
lines.plain: The part where the Project Owner tells forty people that 15 May 2028 is not just a target. It is the date.

lines.text: She sits. Gantt opens a laptop and then a paper notebook, in that order.
lines.plain: Nightingale sits down. Gantt opens a laptop, and then a paper notebook.

lines.text: Minutes. Out within two working days. Anything raised as a risk, an issue, a decision or a change goes into the log as well, not only into the minutes.
lines.plain: I will write the minutes. They go out within two working days. Any risk, issue, decision or change raised here also goes into the correct project log, not only into the minutes.
g: Minutes of Meeting
the written record of who attended, what was decided, and who does what next
ref: Send out the Minutes of Meeting (MoM) to the relevant stakeholders. The minutes should include a summary of project issues raised, risks identified, decisions taken and changes proposed.

lines.text: Who is the empty row for?
lines.plain: Who are the empty seats at the back for?

lines.text: The vendor.
lines.plain: For the company that will build the system.

lines.text: There is no vendor. There are three bids and an evaluation panel that first meets on the ninth of September.
lines.plain: There is no vendor yet. Three companies have sent offers. The panel that evaluates them meets for the first time on 9 September.

lines.text: Item one. Handbook and Work Plan at the level this room can use and no deeper. Seven work packages. Three thousand one hundred person-days. Eight point four million. Release one, twenty-sixth of March 2027. Release two, the seventeenth of December. Parallel run from January 2028. Go-live the fifteenth of May.
lines.plain: Item one. I present the Project Handbook and the Project Work Plan at the level of detail this room needs, and no more. Seven work packages. 3,100 person-days. 8.4 million euro. Release 1 on 26 March 2027. Release 2 on 17 December 2027. Parallel run from January 2028. Go-live on 15 May 2028.
g: work package
a named block of project work with its own effort, owner and dates
ref: Present the Project Handbook and the Project Work Plan with the appropriate level of detail.

lines.text: Then a question that is not on your agenda. When an architect tells me a screen cannot be built the way loan administration actually works, who wins?
lines.plain: Now a question that is not on your agenda. An architect tells me a screen cannot work the way my team really works. Who decides?

lines.text: It is item four and you have opened it early. We agree the conflict resolution process this morning, all of us. Then I present the escalation procedure, which is not open, because Florence signed it in June.
lines.plain: That is item four. You have started it early. This morning we all agree the process for settling disagreements. Then I present the escalation procedure. That one is not open for discussion, because Florence approved it in June.
g: escalation procedure
the agreed route for taking a disagreement up to a higher level of the project
ref: Agree on the conflict resolution process and present the escalation procedure.

lines.text: Agree. Meaning a vote?
lines.plain: You say agree. Do you mean we vote on it?

lines.text: Meaning we settle now that a disagreement is worked where it arises, in writing, for five working days, with Grace and me copied. On the sixth day it goes up. Where up goes is section three point five and you have all had it since June.
lines.plain: I mean we agree now that a disagreement is worked on at the level where it starts, in writing, for five working days, with Grace and me in copy. On the sixth day it is escalated. The route upwards is in Handbook section 3.5, which you have all had since June.

lines.text: Five days. Some of us can fall out considerably faster than that.
lines.plain: Five days is generous. Some of us can start an argument much faster than that.

lines.text: Item six will say that I am independent of the Project Manager. Say it in July. By September nobody remembers reading it.
lines.plain: Item six will state that I work independently of the Project Manager. Say that clearly in July. By September, nobody remembers reading it.

lines.text: Items five and six, then. Stakeholder Matrix. Risk, issue and change management. Quality assurance and control, and who does which.
lines.plain: So, items five and six. The Project Stakeholder Matrix. Then the risk, issue and change management processes. Then the quality assurance and quality control activities, and who performs each of them.
ref: Present the Risk Management, Issue Management and Project Change Management processes as well as the Quality Assurance & Control activities.

lines.text: And item seven is where I get to say what I need from you.
lines.plain: And item seven is where I say what I need from you.

lines.text: Item seven is where I say what I expect of the Core Team. I will take yours in the same twenty minutes and I would rather have it in the room than in a corridor in November.
lines.plain: Item seven is where I explain what I expect from the Project Core Team. I will also listen to what you expect from me, in the same twenty minutes. I would rather hear it here than in a corridor in November.
g: Project Core Team
the people who do the project work and produce the deliverables, coordinated by the Project Manager
ref: Clarify the expectations of the Project Core Team (PCT).

lines.text: Ground rules are item eight and I have brought a flipchart, because a thing written on a flipchart gets argued with and a thing on a slide does not.
lines.plain: Ground rules are item eight. I brought a flipchart. People argue with something written on a flipchart. They do not argue with a slide.
ref: Agree on the team's ground rules

lines.text: First rule. Nothing is real until it is in a log. A risk in the corridor is a conversation. A risk in the Risk Log has an owner, a score and a strategy.
lines.plain: First ground rule. Nothing is real until it is written in a log. A risk mentioned in the corridor is only a conversation. A risk in the Risk Log has an owner, a score and a response strategy.

lines.text: Second. If it has a screen my people touch, my people see it before anyone says it is done.
lines.plain: Second rule. If it has a screen that my staff use, my staff must see it before anyone calls it finished.

lines.text: Third. Nobody books my two business experts without asking me first. They have a quarter-end and it does not move for anyone in this room.
lines.plain: Third rule. Nobody books my two business experts without asking me first. They have quarter-end work, and that work moves for nobody here.

lines.text: Nightingale has not looked at the flipchart once. She is looking at the row of empty chairs at the back of the room.
lines.plain: Nightingale has not looked at the flipchart at all. She is looking at the empty row of chairs at the back.

lines.text: Levallois will win this tender. Everyone in this room knows it. Should they be sitting in it?
lines.plain: Levallois Systems will probably win this tender. Everyone here knows that. Should they be in the room today?

choice.prompt: Three bids are open, the evaluation panel meets in September, and the empty chairs are at the back of your kick-off. Forty people are waiting for your answer.
choice.promptPlain: Three offers are still open. The evaluation panel meets in September. The empty chairs are at the back of your kick-off meeting. Forty people are waiting for your answer.

options.t: No. Required today is the Project Core Team as it exists today, plus Gantt. The contractor joins the team when a contract exists, and is walked through all of this again then.
options.tPlain: No. Today the required people are the Project Core Team as it is now, plus Gantt from the Project Support Office. The contractor joins the team when there is a contract, and then we go through all of this again with them.

reply.text: Then say it at item seven, out loud, so that nobody in September thinks I forgot to invite them.
reply.plain: Then say that clearly at item seven. In September I do not want anyone to think I forgot to invite them.

options.why: The meeting exists to make the whole Project Team aware of the project's key elements and rules (p.56). Required participants are the Project Core Team, and the Project Manager Assistant and Project Support Office if they are part of the project; other roles attend optionally as the project needs. On 10 July the contractor is not part of the project — there are three bids and no contract. The inputs to this meeting are the Business Case, Charter, Handbook, Work Plan, all plans and logs and the requirements documents; handing that set to one bidder during a live evaluation is a procurement failure before it is a method failure. When the team changes, you onboard the new part of it.
options.whyPlain: This meeting makes the whole Project Team aware of the project's rules (page 56). The required people are the Project Core Team, plus the Project Manager Assistant and the Project Support Office if the project has them. Other people may come if the project needs them. On 10 July there is no contractor, only three offers. The meeting uses the Business Case, Charter, Handbook, Work Plan, all plans and logs, and the requirements documents. Giving all of that to one bidder during an open tender is wrong. When the team changes, you brief the new members then.
ref: Project Core Team (PCT) — Required participants.

options.t: Yes. Invite the Levallois bid team as observers. They will win, and they will need the ground rules more than anyone in this room.
options.tPlain: Yes. Invite the Levallois bid team to watch. They will probably win, and they need these ground rules more than anyone here.

reply.text: Three bids. One of them sitting in our risk register. I would quite like to still have a division in October.
reply.plain: There are three bidders. You would seat one of them in front of our risk register. I would prefer to still have a division in October.

options.why: Other project roles or stakeholders attend optionally, as per the project's needs (p.56) — a bidder in a live evaluation is not a project role and the project has no need it can defend. The meeting's inputs include every plan and log the project has. There is also a plainer point: the Executing Kick-off is for the team that will do the work, and on this date that team does not include Levallois.
options.whyPlain: Other roles and stakeholders may attend if the project needs them (page 56). A company still bidding is not a project role, and there is no need the project can defend here. This meeting uses every plan and log the project has. There is a simpler point too: this kick-off is for the team doing the work, and on this date Levallois is not part of that team.
ref: Other project roles or stakeholders — Optional participation (as per the project's needs).

options.t: Step back and let Florence chair the whole meeting. The Steering Committee is Accountable for the Executing Kick-off, so its chair should be running it.
options.tPlain: Step back and let Florence lead the whole meeting. The Steering Committee is Accountable for the Executing Kick-off, so the person who chairs that committee should run it.

reply.text: Then who is left to answer for the eight items, and who do I chase when item three is not presented?
reply.plain: Then who answers for the eight agenda items, and who do I contact when item three is not presented?

options.why: The RASCI row for the Executing Kick-off Meeting is AGB I, PSC A, PO C, BM S/C, BIG C, SP C, PM R, PCT C. Accountable is not the same as doing it: the Steering Committee answers for the meeting having happened properly, and the Key Participants table gives the Project Manager exactly one job — organises the meeting. The Project Owner here is only Consulted, which is a genuine surprise to most people the first time they read it.
options.whyPlain: The RASCI row for this meeting is: governance body Informed, Steering Committee Accountable, Project Owner Consulted, Business Manager supports and is consulted, business group consulted, Solution Provider consulted, Project Manager Responsible, Project Core Team consulted. Accountable does not mean doing the work. The committee answers for the meeting happening properly. The guide gives the Project Manager one job here: organise the meeting. Note that the Project Owner is only Consulted, which surprises most readers.
ref: This meeting ensures that the whole Project Team is aware of the project's key elements and rules.

options.t: Drop items four and five and give the time back. These are senior people who have worked together for years; twenty minutes on conflict resolution reads as an insult.
options.tPlain: Remove items four and five and give the time back. These are senior people who have worked together for years. Twenty minutes on conflict resolution will feel like an insult.

reply.text: Then when the architect and I disagree in November, we will invent a process in November. Badly, and in front of a deadline.
reply.plain: Then when the architect and I disagree in November, we will invent a process in November. We will do it badly, and under time pressure.

options.why: Agreeing the conflict resolution process and presenting the escalation procedure is step 4 of the meeting, and presenting the Project Stakeholder Matrix is step 5 (p.56). They are agreed in July precisely because they are needed in November, when the room is no longer friendly and nobody has the appetite to design a fair process. The Executing Kick-off is the only scheduled moment where the whole team agrees these rules together.
options.whyPlain: Agreeing the conflict resolution process and presenting the escalation procedure is step 4 of this meeting. Presenting the Project Stakeholder Matrix is step 5 (page 56). You agree them in July because you need them in November, when people are angry and nobody wants to design a fair process. This kick-off is the only planned moment when the whole team agrees these rules together.
ref: Agree on the conflict resolution process and present the escalation procedure.

you.o: Project Manager. Responsible for organising and running the Executing Kick-off Meeting.
you.k: Knows the Handbook and Work Plan were baselined on 26 June and the RfE gate passed on 3 July.
you.w: Wants the conflict resolution process and the ground rules agreed out loud, by this room, today.
you.f: Afraid the tender result is treated as already known and someone acts on it.

nightingale.o: Project Owner and chair of the Project Steering Committee, which is Accountable for this meeting.
nightingale.k: Knows the go-live date, the budget, and that three bids are open until September.
nightingale.w: Wants to chair, wants ninety minutes, and wants the May 2028 date heard by everyone.
nightingale.f: Afraid the project drifts into an IT programme she can no longer steer.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Accountable for the deliverables; sits on the evaluation panel.
leonardo.k: Knows the three bids and knows Levallois is the strongest on paper.
leonardo.w: Wants nobody in this room to behave as if the tender is already decided.
leonardo.f: Afraid a procurement irregularity in July destroys a project he has argued for since 2022.

hopper.o: Business Manager. Supports and is consulted on the kick-off; coordinates the Business Implementation Group.
hopper.k: Knows her division has exactly two people who can be spared, and when quarter-end falls.
hopper.w: Wants a ground rule protecting her two business experts from being booked without her.
hopper.f: Afraid the project quietly consumes operational staff who still have a day job.

curie.o: User Representative. Consulted; signs off user-facing documents and acceptance criteria.
curie.k: Knows the 212 requirements her administrators signed, and that nothing has been built yet.
curie.w: Wants a rule that no screen is called done before her people have seen it.
curie.f: Afraid technical people will settle screen design between themselves and inform her later.

gantt.o: Project Support Office. Required to attend; designated to take the Minutes of Meeting.
gantt.k: Knows the Communications Management Plan gives him two working days to publish minutes.
gantt.w: Wants the ground rules on a flipchart, where people will argue with them.
gantt.f: Afraid risks and decisions are raised in the room and never reach a log.

deming.o: Project Quality Assurance. Independent of the Project Manager; establishes the quality standards.
deming.k: Knows the Quality Management Plan was approved with the Handbook on 26 June.
deming.w: Wants his independence stated in July, in front of the whole team.
deming.f: Afraid he is treated as the Project Manager's reviewer rather than the project's.

lovelace.o: Business Analyst on the Project Core Team. Required participant; owns the requirements artefacts.
lovelace.k: Knows the 212 requirements are documented but not yet frozen or traced to tests.
lovelace.w: Wants a date when requirements stop moving, so she can write acceptance tests.
lovelace.f: Afraid expectations flow one way and nobody ever asks what the team needs.

note: Guide check: section 7.1, p.56. The Executing Kick-off Meeting opens the Executing Phase and ensures the whole Project Team is aware of the project's key elements and rules. The Project Manager organises it. The Project Core Team are required participants; the Project Manager Assistant and the Project Support Office are required to attend if they are part of the project; other project roles and stakeholders participate optionally, as per the project's needs. During the meeting: designate someone to take the Minutes of Meeting including action points; present the Project Handbook and Project Work Plan at the appropriate level of detail; present the Communications Management Plan; agree the conflict resolution process and present the escalation procedure; present the Project Stakeholder Matrix; present the Risk, Issue and Project Change Management processes and the Quality Assurance and Control activities; clarify the expectations of the Project Core Team; agree the team's ground rules. Afterwards the minutes go out, and the issues, risks, decisions and changes they contain are also recorded in the relevant logs. RASCI: AGB I, PSC A, PO C, BM S/C, BIG C, SP C, PM R, PCT C. Approver: the Project Steering Committee is Accountable; the Project Manager is Responsible. Page 56.
notePlain: Rule: the Executing Kick-off Meeting starts the Executing Phase. Its purpose is to make sure the whole Project Team knows the project's key elements and rules. The Project Manager organises it. The Project Core Team must attend. The Project Manager Assistant and the Project Support Office must attend if the project has them. Other people attend only if the project needs them. In the meeting you: name someone to write the minutes; present the Project Handbook and the Project Work Plan at the right level of detail; present the Communications Management Plan; agree how conflicts will be settled and present the escalation route; present the Project Stakeholder Matrix; present the risk, issue and change processes and the quality activities; explain what you expect from the Project Core Team; and agree the team's ground rules. After the meeting the minutes go out, and every risk, issue, decision and change in them also goes into the correct log. RASCI: Steering Committee Accountable, Project Manager Responsible, Project Owner Consulted, Business Manager supports and is consulted, and the governance body is only Informed. Page 56.

title: What gets counted
where: ESM, Kirchberg — Project Support Office, third floor

lines.text: The Project Support Office is two desks, four filing cabinets and a window facing the car park. Gantt has printed the Work Plan across six sheets of A3 and taped them to the wall in the wrong order, then fixed it.
lines.plain: The Project Support Office has two desks, four filing cabinets and a window that looks at the car park. Gantt printed the Project Work Plan on six large sheets and taped them to the wall. He put them up in the wrong order and then corrected it.

lines.text: That is the baseline. Twenty-sixth of June, version one point zero, approved. One copy. It does not move.
lines.plain: That is the baseline. Approved on 26 June, version 1.0. There is one copy and it does not change.
g: baseline
the approved version of scope, dates and cost that all later progress is measured against
ref: Use the baselined Project Work Plan as a reference for monitoring project performance.

lines.text: And the copy on my drive?
lines.plain: What about the copy on my own drive?

lines.text: Is a photograph of it.
lines.plain: That is only a picture of it. It is not the baseline.

lines.text: There is nothing to measure yet. Two weeks in, no contract, no build. That is exactly why we are doing this today.
lines.plain: There is nothing to measure yet. We are two weeks into the phase, with no contract and no build work. That is exactly why we are doing this today.

lines.text: You have called a meeting about measuring nothing.
lines.plain: So you have called a meeting about measuring nothing.

lines.text: I have called a meeting about what the word done will mean in March. Agreed in July it is a definition. Agreed in March it is an argument with a release in it.
lines.plain: I have called a meeting about what the word done will mean in March. If we agree it in July, it is a definition. If we agree it in March, it is an argument, and there is a release waiting behind it.

lines.text: Florence knows we are doing this?
lines.plain: Does Florence know that we are doing this?

lines.text: It is her name in the accountable column. My job is to hand her something she can read on a Tuesday without a translator. She sees the shape of it next week.
lines.plain: Florence is Accountable for monitoring. My job is to give her something she can read on a Tuesday without help. She will see the format next week.
ref: Project Manager (PM) — Undertakes all project monitoring activities.

lines.text: Then ban percentages. Ninety per cent complete means a developer feels good on a Thursday. It has never once meant that nine tenths of the work is behind us.
lines.plain: Then do not allow percentages. Ninety per cent complete means a developer felt good on a Thursday. It has never meant that nine tenths of the work is finished.
g: percent complete
a self-reported guess at how far a task has got; easy to give, hard to check

lines.text: So a task is at zero or at a hundred, and it reaches a hundred when somebody who did not build it says so.
lines.plain: So a task is either at zero or at one hundred. It reaches one hundred only when somebody who did not build it confirms it.
ref: Key outputs—i.e. completed and verified deliverables, and milestones achieved as planned.

lines.text: Verified by whom, in July, before there is anything to verify?
lines.plain: Verified by whom? It is July, and there is nothing yet to verify.

lines.text: Named now, task by task, in the plan. Ada for specifications. Marie's people for anything with a screen. Grace for anything that touches a payment instruction.
lines.plain: We name the verifier now, task by task, in the Project Work Plan. Ada for specifications. Marie Curie's staff for anything with a screen. Grace for anything that touches a payment instruction.

lines.text: Then I want four things every second Tuesday, in the same shape every time. Critical path tasks and the ones about to become critical. Deliverables finished and verified. Days burned against days planned. And the four logs.
lines.plain: Then I want four things every second Tuesday, always in the same format. First, the critical path tasks and the tasks about to become critical. Second, deliverables that are finished and verified. Third, days used compared with days planned. Fourth, the four project logs.
g: critical path
the chain of tasks whose delay would delay the whole project
burn rate
how fast the project is using up its person-days or its money
ref: Tasks—i.e. the status of critical and next critical path tasks.

lines.text: That is four. What about people?
lines.plain: That is four things. What about the people?

lines.text: People is not a number.
lines.plain: People cannot be turned into a number.

lines.text: People is the first thing that goes wrong and the last thing anybody writes down. Ask me in February how the test team is and I will tell you before any of your columns do.
lines.plain: People are the first thing that goes wrong and the last thing anybody writes down. Ask me in February how the test team is feeling. I will know before any of your columns show it.
ref: People—i.e. team morale, stakeholder engagement, overall project dynamics and productivity.

lines.text: Then it is the fifth thing and I collect it by walking around, not on a form. Half of what I will need never arrives at a scheduled meeting.
lines.plain: Then people is the fifth thing. I will collect it by walking around and talking, not with a form. Half of what I need will never come to me in a planned meeting.
ref: Regularly exchange information about the project's current status and next steps with the Project Core Team (PCT) at formal and informal meetings.

lines.text: Second Tuesday. My architects are already in two stand-ups and a sprint review, and they will be in a contractor's ceremony as well by October.
lines.plain: Every second Tuesday. My architects already attend two short daily meetings and a sprint review. By October they will also attend the contractor's own meetings.
g: sprint
a short fixed working period, usually two weeks, ending in something that can be shown

lines.text: They report once. Gantt takes the sprint data and reshapes it. Nobody on CASTOR types the same number into two systems.
lines.plain: They will report once. Gantt takes the sprint data and puts it into our format. On Project CASTOR, nobody types the same number into two different systems.

lines.text: I want that in writing.
lines.plain: I want that written down.

lines.text: Handbook, section five. In writing since June, read by nobody, which is the other reason we are all here.
lines.plain: It is in the Project Handbook, section 5. It has been written down since June and nobody read it. That is the other reason we are meeting today.

lines.text: And when the number is bad?
lines.plain: And what happens when the number is bad?

lines.text: Then it is bad on the same Tuesday as everything else. Monitoring decides nothing. It only makes sure that when we do decide, we are deciding about the project and not about a mood.
lines.plain: Then it is reported as bad on the same Tuesday as everything else. Monitoring does not decide anything. It only makes sure that when we do decide, we decide about the real project and not about how people feel.
ref: Track the project performance against the baseline in order to facilitate reporting and controlling.

lines.text: Leonardo studies the six sheets for a while. Then he takes a pencil out of his jacket and, without asking anybody, draws a short line down the margin of sheet four.
lines.plain: Leonardo looks at the six sheets for a while. Then he takes a pencil from his jacket and draws a short line in the margin of sheet four, without asking permission.

lines.text: Data migration. Four hundred and eighty person-days, one owner, no verifier. Put a name there before you measure anything at all.
lines.plain: Look at data migration. It has 480 person-days and one owner, but no verifier. Write a name there before you measure anything.
ref: Project Core Team (PCT) — Contributes information on project progress.

you.o: Project Manager. Responsible for all project monitoring activities across scope, schedule, cost and quality.
you.k: Knows the Work Plan was baselined on 26 June and that nothing has been built yet.
you.w: Wants the definition of done fixed now, while it costs nothing to agree.
you.f: Afraid March arrives with self-reported percentages and no verified deliverable anywhere.

gantt.o: Project Support Office. Holds the baselined Work Plan and assists with document change control.
gantt.k: Knows every version of every plan and where the single controlled copy lives.
gantt.w: Wants four fixed data items every second Tuesday, always in the same shape.
gantt.f: Afraid of a project run from three private spreadsheets that disagree.

hopper.o: Business Manager. Consulted on monitoring; verifies anything touching a payment instruction.
hopper.k: Knows her division's calendar and which of her staff are already stretched.
hopper.w: Wants team morale treated as data, not as an optional soft extra.
hopper.f: Afraid the numbers look healthy right up to the week the test team breaks.

lovelace.o: Business Analyst on the Project Core Team. Contributes progress information; verifies specifications.
lovelace.k: Knows how percent-complete reporting behaved on the collateral register project.
lovelace.w: Wants percentage progress banned and replaced by verified completion.
lovelace.f: Afraid she will be asked to test against a specification that is still moving.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Informed on monitoring; accountable for the deliverables being measured.
leonardo.k: Knows his architects already report into two other cadences and will soon have a third.
leonardo.w: Wants one reporting route for his people, not a new form every fortnight.
leonardo.f: Afraid data migration has 480 person-days, one owner and nobody to check it.

note: Guide check: chapter 9, pp.69-70. Monitor and Control activities run for the whole project but peak during the Executing Phase, and they have three verbs: Manage the processes defined in the plans, Monitor performance against the baseline, and Control by devising and implementing corrective actions. Monitor Project Performance (section 9.1, p.70) collects information on the project's progress and overall health. Step 1 is to use the baselined Project Work Plan as the reference. What is gathered is named: the status of critical and next critical path tasks; key outputs, meaning completed and verified deliverables and milestones achieved as planned; resource utilisation against budget; the status and evolution of the logs; and people, meaning morale, stakeholder engagement and productivity. Information is exchanged with the Project Core Team at formal and informal meetings. RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM C, BIG C, SP I, PM R, PCT C. Approver: none — this is an activity, not a document. The Project Owner is Accountable, the Project Manager Responsible. Page 70.
notePlain: Rule: Monitor and Control runs through the whole project but is strongest during Executing. It has three parts: manage the processes in the plans, monitor performance against the baseline, and control by planning and applying corrective actions. Monitor Project Performance (page 70) collects information about progress and project health. Step 1: use the baselined Project Work Plan as your reference. You collect: the critical path tasks and the ones about to become critical; key outputs, meaning deliverables that are finished and verified, and milestones reached as planned; resources used against budget; the state of the project logs; and people, meaning morale, engagement and productivity. You exchange this information with the Project Core Team in both formal and informal meetings. RASCI: Project Owner Accountable, Project Manager Responsible, Business Manager and business group Consulted, Project Core Team Consulted. There is no approver, because this is an activity and not a document. Page 70.

title: Ninety per cent, and one line that says partially
where: ESM, Kirchberg — room Spaak, fifth floor

lines.text: Gustave Eiffel has been in the building for forty minutes and has already asked where the goods lift is. The contract was signed a week ago. He takes the chair with a view of the door and keeps his coat on.
lines.plain: Gustave Eiffel has been in the building for forty minutes. He has already asked where the goods lift is. The contract was signed one week ago. He sits where he can see the door and keeps his coat on.

lines.text: Before anything else. Who may speak to my engineers?
lines.plain: First question, before anything else. Who is allowed to talk to my engineers?

lines.text: Me, through you. Everyone else, through me, through you.
lines.plain: I speak to them through you. Everyone else speaks to me, and then I speak to you.

lines.text: Then we shall get along. My status report reaches you by the fifth of each month. If it is late, it is late because I am late, not because someone in your building is thinking about it.

note: Guide check: section 7.2, p.57. The objective of project coordination is to facilitate progress by continuously providing information to the Project Core Team and supporting the completion of assigned work. It covers allocating resources to activities, performing regular quality checks of interim results, maintaining communication with all team members, and keeping people motivated through leadership, negotiation, conflict resolution and human resource techniques. Coordination begins with the initiation of the project and ends with its closing, but its intensity peaks during Executing. The steps include assigning tasks as per the Project Work Plan, providing the team with the information it needs, verifying the completion of tasks and accepting interim work deliverables in line with predefined acceptance criteria, and managing project team dynamics. The output is signed off work assignments. RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM S, BIG I, SP I, PM R, PCT I. Approver: none — the Project Owner is Accountable and the Project Manager Responsible, with the Business Manager supporting depending on the project. Page 57.
notePlain: Rule: project coordination exists to keep the work moving. You give the Project Core Team the information it needs and you support them in finishing the work assigned to them. It includes putting people on activities, checking the quality of interim results regularly, keeping in contact with everyone, and keeping people motivated through leadership, negotiation and conflict resolution. Coordination starts when the project starts and ends when it closes, but it is strongest during the Executing Phase. The steps include: assign tasks as written in the Project Work Plan; give the team the information it needs; check that tasks are complete and accept interim deliverables against acceptance criteria agreed in advance; and manage how the team works together. The output is signed off work assignments. RASCI: Project Owner Accountable, Project Manager Responsible, Business Manager supports. There is no approver. Page 57.

note: Guide check: section 9.5, pp.74-75. Requirements management runs through the whole lifecycle: specify, evaluate, approve, monitor implementation, validate. A requirement is a capability a product or service must have to satisfy a stakeholder's need. Requirements should describe the need and not the solution, avoiding technology- or solution-oriented statements. For each requirement there should be a corresponding test to validate its acceptance, documented in the Deliverables Acceptance Plan, the Deliverables Acceptance Checklist or the Quality Review Checklist. The agreed and approved requirements of all stakeholders constitute the project's baseline scope, and any change to them must follow the change management process in the Change Management Plan. The Business Manager provides the information needed to draft the requirements and approves them; User Representatives participate in gathering and validation; the Business Analyst, a member of the Project Core Team and not a PM² role of its own, does much of the documentation work. Even if requirements were gathered before the project started, it remains the Project Manager's responsibility to manage them properly. RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM C, BIG C, SP I, PM R, PCT S. Approver: the Project Owner is Accountable; the Business Manager approves the requirements themselves. Pages 74 and 75.
notePlain: Rule: requirements management runs through the whole project. The steps are: specify, evaluate, approve, monitor the implementation, and validate. A requirement is something the product must be able to do so that a stakeholder's need is met. Write the need, not the solution. Do not write technology or design into a requirement. Every requirement needs a matching test that proves it has been met, written in the Deliverables Acceptance Plan, the Deliverables Acceptance Checklist or the Quality Review Checklist. Once all stakeholders have agreed and approved the requirements, those requirements are the project's baseline scope. After that, they can only change through the change process. The Business Manager gives the information for drafting and approves the requirements. User Representatives help gather and validate them. The Business Analyst is a member of the Project Core Team, not a separate PM² role, and does much of the writing. Even requirements collected before the project began are the Project Manager's to manage. RASCI: Project Owner Accountable, Project Manager Responsible, Project Core Team supports, Business Manager and business group Consulted. Pages 74 and 75.

note: Guide check: Control Schedule, section 9.2, p.71 and Control Cost, section 9.3, p.72. Schedule control ensures tasks are carried out as scheduled; the Project Manager tracks the difference between planned, actual and forecast dates. Only approved project changes are incorporated into the Project Work Plan. If the schedule is at risk beyond the predefined thresholds, the Project Steering Committee must be informed, corrective actions devised, agreed and implemented, and affected stakeholders notified. Cost control manages costs against the cost and effort baseline. The project budget must have been approved by the Project Owner at the beginning of the project. Differences between budgeted and actual costs are evaluated and communicated, with approval for significant differences secured from the Project Owner. If considerable overruns are foreseen they must be justified, reported to and approved by the Project Owner or the Appropriate Governance Body. If the budget must be considerably revised, this must be justified and documented, and formal approval from the Appropriate Governance Body is required before the affected plans can be re-baselined. RASCI, both rows identically: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM C, BIG C, SP I, PM R, PCT C. Approver: the Project Owner is Accountable for both; the Appropriate Governance Body approves any re-baselining. Pages 71 and 72.
notePlain: Rule: Control Schedule (page 71) makes sure tasks happen when planned. The Project Manager tracks the difference between planned, actual and forecast dates. Only approved changes go into the Project Work Plan. If the schedule is at risk beyond the agreed limits, tell the Steering Committee, design and agree corrective actions, carry them out, and inform the affected stakeholders. Control Cost (page 72) keeps spending inside the cost and effort baseline. The Project Owner must have approved the budget at the start. You measure and report the difference between budget and actual cost, and get the Project Owner's approval for significant differences. Large forecast overruns must be justified, reported and approved by the Project Owner or the Appropriate Governance Body. If the budget must be revised substantially, write down the justification, and get formal approval from the Appropriate Governance Body before any plan is re-baselined. RASCI, the same for both: Project Owner Accountable, Project Manager Responsible, Business Manager, business group and core team Consulted. Pages 71 and 72.

Step 4, implement: incorporate the actions into the Project Work Plan and update the related documentation and logs. Step 5, control. RASCI: AGB I, PSC C, PO A, BM S, BIG I, SP I, PM R, PCT C. Approver: the Project Owner and/or the Project Steering Committee. The Project Manager is Responsible for the process and for the record, and Accountable for neither the yes nor the no. Pages 76 and 77.
